entries.narration: Let's start with the application we will follow through the whole course: a small online shop. A shopper opens the page for product p one thousand and one. The browser asks Route fifty three, the D N S service, for the shop's address, then sends an H T T P S request to a load balancer. The load balancer passes it to one of our app servers, which reads the product from the orders database and links to its image in object storage. Three ideas sit inside that picture. First, every one of those resources is on demand. We create it with an A P I call, and we pay while it exists, not for a machine we bought. Second, some of them are managed services. We never patch the load balancer, and A W S runs the database engine; we only configure them. Third, elasticity. Look at the chart. One app server handles a hundred and fifty requests a second. Overnight, demand is sixty. During the day it is two hundred and forty, and on a sale evening it reaches five hundred and sixty. If we size for the peak, we run four servers all day, which is ninety six server hours. If capacity follows demand, we run one server for eight hours, two for ten, and four for six, which is fifty two server hours, about forty six percent fewer. Now the misconception. The cloud does not scale by itself. You write the scaling rules, a new server takes minutes to be ready, so the evening rise must be anticipated, and account quotas put a ceiling on how many you can start. So the operating model changes who buys hardware, but you still own the design, the configuration, and the bill.

Every A W S service splits the work between two owners, and the split is worth knowing before anything goes wrong. A W S is responsible for security of the cloud: the buildings, the hardware, the host operating systems, and the virtualisation layer that runs your instances. You are responsible for security in the cloud: how you configure things, the code you deploy, who you let in, and your data. The important part is that the line moves with the service. Read the matrix for our ordering app. Our app servers run on E C two, which is infrastructure as a service, so we patch the guest operating system, we install the software, and we set the network rules around each instance. The database runs on R D S. There, A W S patches the operating system and the database engine, but it does so in a maintenance window we choose, and the tables and S Q L are still ours. A Lambda function goes further: A W S runs the runtime, and we own the code and its permissions. S three has no servers for us at all. Yet look at the bottom two rows. Who may access the data, and how it is backed up, are ours for every service on the board. The list on the right turns this into incidents. An unpatched operating system on an app server is our problem. A bucket policy that allows public reads is our problem. A failed disk under the database host is A W S's problem. The misconception to avoid is that managed means secure. A managed service runs correctly, but it does exactly what you configured it to do. So the summary is simple: access and data are always yours, and everything else depends on the service you chose.

Every resource you create lives somewhere, and where it lives decides what can take it down. A Region is a geographic area with its own copy of the services and its own endpoints. Our shop runs in E U west two, which is London. Inside a Region are Availability Zones, groups of data centres with separate power, cooling and networking, close enough for fast links but far enough apart that one local failure should not reach the others. E U west two has three. One small trap: the names A, B and C can point at different physical zones in different accounts in some Regions, so when accounts must agree, they compare zone I Ds instead. Now place the parts of our app. An app server is zonal; it lives in exactly one zone. An S three bucket is Regional; A W S spreads it across zones for us. Our single orders database is placed in one zone, which matters later. And some services are global, outside any one Region: I A M, Route fifty three, and CloudFront. Now the arithmetic. At the evening peak we need four app servers. If we run one per zone, that is three, which is already short, and if a zone fails only two remain. If we run two per zone, that is six. Lose a zone and four remain, which carries the peak. Those two extra servers are the price of surviving a zone failure, and you pay it every hour. The misconception is that multi A Z makes you unstoppable. A Region-wide problem, a bad deployment, or deleted data reaches every zone at once. So decide which boundary you must survive, and pay for exactly the spare capacity that survival needs.

Before we create anything, we need a safe way in. An A W S account is a container: it holds resources, it receives one bill, and it draws a boundary around permissions. Every account has a root user, the email address that created it, and the root user can do everything, including closing the account. So we protect it with multi factor authentication, which A W S now enforces for root users, and we use it only for the handful of tasks that truly need it. Organizations can go further and remove root credentials from member accounts entirely. Daily work happens through I A M Identity Center instead. Follow alex, a developer joining the shop's development account. On the left is alex's configuration. It names the sign-in portal, the account, four four four four, five five five five, six six six six, and the role called ShopDeveloper. Running a w s s s o login opens a browser, where alex enters a password and an M F A code. Then a w s s t s get caller identity asks the Security Token Service a simple question: who am I? Look at the answer. The A R N says assumed role. Alex is not a user with a stored key; alex is holding temporary credentials for a role, and by default that role session lasts one hour, configurable up to twelve, before it must be renewed. The misconception is that an access key in a file is simpler. It is simpler, until it leaks. A long-term key never expires, and it works for whoever finds it. Temporary credentials expire on their own. So the pattern is: root locked away, and people working through one sign-in that hands out short sessions.

Whether you click in the console, type in the C L I, or call an S D K from code, the same thing happens underneath: a signed H T T P S request to an A W S service A P I. Learn to read one, and you can read them all. Take this command. It asks S three, using head object, whether the product file for p one thousand and one exists, and for its metadata, without downloading the body. Read it in three parts. Who: the shop dev profile, which supplies the temporary credentials from our last section. Where: the Region, E U west two, which selects the London endpoint. What: one key in one bucket. Now follow the list. The C L I finds the credentials for the profile. It signs the request with Signature Version four, which binds the signature to the key, the Region and the service. The request travels over H T T P S to the Regional S three endpoint. There, I A M checks whether this identity is allowed the action s three get object on that object's A R N. Head object needs the same permission as reading the object. If it is allowed, we get two hundred O K with headers only: one thousand eight hundred and thirty four bytes, J S O N, and encrypted at rest, which S three does by default for new objects. Notice the A R N shapes on the right. An A R N names a resource exactly, but not every A R N carries every field. S three bucket names are global, so their A R Ns have no Region and no account. I A M is global, so its A R Ns have no Region. A DynamoDB table carries both. The misconception is that the console is a separate system. It calls the same A P Is, under the same permission checks. So every call reduces to identity, Region, resource and action, and the answer is a response or an error that tells you which of the four went wrong.

The last foundation is money, because in the cloud every resource you create is a charge until you delete it. The core rule is that charges follow what exists, not only what is running. Look at the ledger for the shop's development environment. The rates here are hypothetical, chosen to make the arithmetic clear, so check the current pricing pages before you rely on any number. With seven hundred and thirty hours in a month, the running environment costs thirty six dollars and twenty one cents. Now stop the app instance. The compute charge, twenty nine dollars twenty, disappears. But seven dollars and one cent remains, because the thirty gigabyte volume still exists, the Elastic I P is still reserved, the snapshot is still stored, and the product images are still in S three. Stopping is not deleting. To see costs by purpose, we tag resources: project equals shop, environment equals dev, owner equals alex. A tag only appears in cost reports once it is activated as a cost allocation tag, so do that early. Then a budget. Set one for the account, with an alert when actual spending passes eighty percent, and another when the forecast passes one hundred. Here is the misconception. A budget is not a spending cap. Budget data is updated up to three times a day, so an alert can arrive after the money is spent. Budget actions can apply a restrictive policy or stop specific E C two or R D S instances, but they only touch what you configured, and charges like storage keep accruing. So: tag on creation, alert early, and delete what you no longer need. With safe access, a request path, and a ledger, we are ready to make identities and permissions explicit, which is the next chapter.

Every request to A W S is made by a principal, and the first question is always who that principal is. A principal can be the root user, an I A M user with long-term credentials, a session of an I A M role holding temporary credentials, or an A W S service acting for you, such as E C two. Two words get confused here. Authentication proves who you are: a password and an M F A code. Authorisation decides what that proven identity may do, and the rest of this chapter is about authorisation. For people, the modern pattern is federation. A W S does not keep its own password for alex; it trusts the sign-in of the shop's workforce identity provider, through I A M Identity Center. Look at the board. Alex and sam live in the identity source, in groups. Identity Center holds assignments, and an assignment is three things: a group, an account, and a permission set, which is a template of policies. Developers get ShopDeveloper in the dev account, but only ShopReadOnly in production. Operators get ShopOperator in production. When you make an assignment, Identity Center creates a real I A M role in that account, named A W S Reserved S S O followed by the permission set's name and a suffix, and attaches the set's policies. So when alex signs in, alex is not an I A M user anywhere; alex becomes a session of one of those roles. The misconception is that every person needs an I A M user in every account. That multiplies long-term keys, and when someone leaves, every one of those keys must be found. With federation, people sign in once, and accounts only ever see roles.

People are not the only principals. The order A P I running on our app servers also needs to call A W S: it reads product files from S three and sends order events to a queue. The wrong way is to put an access key in a configuration file on the server. The right way is a role. A role is an identity with no password and no key of its own; instead, principals that the role trusts can become it for a while. Every role has two policies, and the board shows both. On the left is the trust policy, the role's front door. It says that only the E C two service, e c two dot amazon a w s dot com, may call s t s assume role on it. On the right is the permissions policy, which says what a session of the role may do: get objects from the catalogue bucket, and send messages to the order events queue. The commands below create the role from those two files, then wrap it in an instance profile, which is how a role is attached to E C two instances. On the server, E C two assumes the role, the instance metadata service version two serves the temporary keys, and the S D K finds them without a single key in our code. The Security Token Service issues these keys, and they expire; an assume role session lasts one hour by default and at most twelve, and on an instance fresh keys arrive before the old ones expire. The misconception is that the trust policy grants access. It does not. It only says who may walk through the front door; what they can do inside is decided by the permissions policy. A role is two policies: who may become it, and what it may then do.

Now let's read a policy properly, because every permission in A W S comes down to statements like these. Each statement answers four questions. Effect: is this an allow or a deny? Action: which A P I calls, written as the service prefix, a colon, and the operation name, like s three get object. Resource: which resources, named by A R N, where a star matches any run of characters. And condition: an optional extra test on the request itself. Here is the order A P I's policy after one change. The app now lists the products in the catalogue, so it needs a second statement. Read them in turn. ReadProducts allows get object on every object whose key starts with products slash. ListProducts allows list bucket, and notice its resource: it is the bucket's own A R N, with no slash and no star, because listing is an action on the bucket, not on an object. Its condition narrows it further: the request's prefix must start with products. SendOrderEvents allows one action on one queue. That difference between the bucket and its objects is the classic mistake. Granting s three star on the bucket's A R N does not reach the objects inside it; objects have their own A R Ns, the bucket name followed by slash and the key, and an object action needs a resource that matches them. So a statement applies to a request only when the action, the resource and every condition all match, and then its effect counts.

With statements in hand, we can predict any decision. Start from the default: every request is denied unless something allows it. Then A W S gathers every policy that applies to the request. If any of them contains an explicit deny that matches, the answer is deny, full stop. If not, at least one allow must match, from an identity policy or a resource policy. And some policy types only cap the result. A permissions boundary, an organization's service control policy, or a session policy can take permissions away, but none of them can grant anything on its own. Let's test it. We add one statement to the order A P I's policy, DenyDrafts, which denies get object on anything under products slash drafts. Now read the matrix. Product one thousand and one is allowed by ReadProducts. The draft product two thousand matches ReadProducts too, but it also matches DenyDrafts, and the deny wins. Private slash costs dot c s v matches no statement at all, so it is an implicit deny. Putting an object is an implicit deny as well, because nothing allows put object. Sending an order event is allowed. These outcomes were checked by running the requests in an emulator with this exact policy. When a real request is denied, the error message names the type of policy that decided, for example an explicit deny in an identity based policy, which tells you where to look. The misconception is that a more specific allow can beat a broader deny. It cannot. Deny wins, and only then does something have to allow.

So far every policy was attached to an identity. A resource policy is attached to the resource instead: a bucket policy, a queue policy, a key policy. Because it sits on the resource, it must say who it is talking about, so it has a principal element. Our case: the audit account, seven seven seven seven, eight eight eight eight, nine nine nine nine, has an Auditor role that must read nightly reports from a bucket in production. On the left is the bucket policy in production. It names the Auditor role's A R N and allows get object on the reports. On the right is the Auditor role's own identity policy in the audit account, allowing the same read. Now the table. Within one account, an allow from either side is enough: an identity policy alone, or a resource policy alone. Across accounts, it is different. A W S evaluates the request in both accounts, and both must allow. The bucket owner must name the caller, and the caller's account must permit its principal to make the call. Remove either policy and the auditor is denied. There are exceptions even within one account: a role can only be assumed if its trust policy allows it, and a K M S key is only usable if its key policy permits it. The same idea governs services talking to services. When S three sends event notifications to an S Q S queue, the queue's resource policy must allow the S three service, and it should be scoped to our bucket with a source A R N condition, so that no one else's bucket can use that trust. The misconception is that A W S services are trusted automatically. They are not. Across accounts, and between services, both owners must agree.

Inside one account, separating development from production depends on every policy being written perfectly. Accounts give a stronger boundary. Resources, permissions and service quotas all belong to an account, so an account is the hardest wall A W S offers. A W S Organizations groups accounts together. One account, the management account, creates the organization; it should do little else. Accounts are placed in organisational units, O Us, which can be nested, and policies attach to an O U once and apply to every account below it. The whole organization pays one consolidated bill, while costs remain visible per account. Here is the shop's structure. At the root sits the management account. A Security O U holds the audit account, which will collect logs and run security tools. A Workloads O U contains two O Us, Prod and Dev, each with one account. Now read the table of what this separates. Permissions: an administrator in dev has no rights in production unless production grants them. Resources: a script that deletes every bucket it can see in dev cannot see production's buckets. Quotas: a load test in dev cannot use up production's limits. Bills: each account's cost is visible on its own. The misconception is that tags or naming conventions separate environments. Tags are labels; a policy mistake crosses them easily. Accounts are walls. So give each environment its own account, and group them with O Us.

The last layer is guardrails: limits set once, at the organization, that no account can exceed. There are two kinds. A service control policy, an S C P, limits what principals in member accounts can do. A resource control policy, an R C P, limits what anyone can do to resources in member accounts, whoever the caller is. Neither of them ever grants a permission, and neither affects the management account, which is one more reason to keep that account almost empty. On the left is an S C P attached to the Workloads O U. It denies every action outside E U west two, except the listed global services such as I A M, Route fifty three and CloudFront, which are not tied to our Region. On the right is an R C P. It denies any S three access by principals outside our organization, unless an A W S service is acting for us. Even if someone later writes a bucket policy that opens a bucket to the world, this guardrail still blocks outsiders. R C Ps launched for S three, S T S, K M S, S Q S and Secrets Manager, and have since added services, so check the current list. The table puts every policy type in one place: only identity and resource policies grant; boundaries, S C Ps and R C Ps only limit. Finally, ownership of the audit trail. Rather than run security tools from the management account, a member account, our audit account, is made the delegated administrator for services such as GuardDuty and Security Hub, and it collects the organization's logs. The misconception is that an S C P gives production its permissions. It does not; roles still need an allow. Guardrails cap, and only identity and resource policies grant. Authorisation still says nothing about whether a request can reach its target, so next we trace the network paths requests must travel.

Before we can trace a request through a network, we need its addresses. An I P version four address is thirty two bits, written as four numbers, like ten dot twenty dot eleven dot thirty seven. A range of addresses is written in C I D R notation: an address, a slash, and a number saying how many leading bits are fixed. A slash sixteen fixes sixteen bits and leaves sixteen free, which is sixty five thousand five hundred and thirty six addresses. A slash twenty four leaves eight bits free, which is two hundred and fifty six. Addresses find a machine; ports find a program on it. H T T P S listens on four four three. Our app servers listen on eight zero eight zero, PostgreSQL on five four three two, and D N S on fifty three. T C P gives an ordered, acknowledged stream; U D P sends single packets, which is why D N S often uses it. Now the shop's plan, computed rather than asserted. The production V P C is ten dot twenty dot zero dot zero slash sixteen. The code cuts it into nine slash twenty four subnets: public, app and data tiers, one of each per Availability Zone. A W S reserves five addresses in every subnet, the first four and the last, so each slash twenty four has two hundred and fifty one usable addresses. The code also finds which subnet holds ten dot twenty dot eleven dot thirty seven, app b, and confirms that no two ranges overlap. The misconception is that a bigger range is always safer. The real risk is overlap: two networks using the same addresses can never be joined later. So plan ranges once, check them with code, and never let them overlap.

A V P C, a virtual private cloud, is your own private network inside one Region. It owns an address range, and every network resource you create lives inside it. A V P C spans all the Availability Zones of its Region, but a subnet does not. A subnet is a slice of the V P C's range placed in exactly one zone. And the thing that actually connects a server to a subnet is its elastic network interface, an E N I, which sits in one subnet and takes its private address from that subnet's range. Look at the layout for shop prod. The V P C is ten dot twenty dot zero dot zero slash sixteen, in E U west two. Each of the three zones gets three subnets, one per tier: a public subnet for the load balancer and N A T gateways, an app subnet for the order A P I servers, and a data subnet for the database. So the app server in zone b has an E N I in app b, with the address ten dot twenty dot eleven dot thirty seven from our calculation. Why tiers? Because each tier will get different routes and different filters, and those attach to subnets and interfaces. And why repeat them in every zone? Because, as we saw in chapter one, surviving the loss of a zone means having capacity in the others. The misconception is that one subnet can span the Region. It cannot; if you want a tier in three zones, you create three subnets. So: one V P C per environment, and one subnet per tier per zone.

Addresses say where a packet is going; route tables say which way to send it. Every subnet is associated with one route table, a list of destination ranges and targets. Every table contains a local route for the V P C's own range, so instances in the same V P C can always reach each other's addresses. An internet gateway, attached to the V P C, is its door to the internet, and a default route, zero dot zero dot zero dot zero slash zero, pointing at it is what makes a subnet public. Look at the two tables. The public subnets send everything outside the V P C to the internet gateway. The app subnets have three routes: local, a route to the development V P C through a peering connection, which we meet in section nine, and a default route to a N A T gateway, which is the next section. When a destination matches more than one route, the most specific one wins, the one with the longest prefix. The code applies that rule. Ten dot twenty dot twenty dot fifteen, a database address, matches local. Ten dot thirty dot four dot nine matches both the slash sixteen to dev and the default route, and the slash sixteen is more specific, so it goes over the peering. The payment provider's address matches only the default, so it goes to the N A T gateway. The misconception is that the order of rows in the table decides. It does not; the prefix length decides. So to predict a packet's next hop, find the subnet's route table and pick the longest matching prefix.

Now an incident, the one the plan asks us to diagnose. The order A P I runs in the private app subnets, and it must call a payment provider at api dot payments dot example dot com. The call times out after five seconds. Read the route table, as the comment does: rt app a contains only the local route. There is no path out of the V P C at all, so the packets have nowhere to go, and a timeout, rather than a refusal, is the typical symptom. We do not want the app servers to be reachable from the internet, so we will not give them public addresses or a route to the internet gateway. Instead we add a N A T gateway. It sits in a public subnet, it has an Elastic I P, and it translates the private servers' outgoing connections so they appear to come from that one public address. The commands allocate the address, create the N A T gateway in public a, and add a default route from the app subnet's table to it. Replies to connections the servers started come back through the N A T; connections started from the internet cannot come in. N A T gateways are zonal by default, so one per zone keeps each zone's outbound traffic independent of the others. Now the table. A server in a public subnet with a public address can call out and be called. In a public subnet without a public address, it can do neither. Private with no N A T route, neither. Private with a N A T route, outbound only. The misconception is that putting something in a public subnet makes it reachable. It also needs a public address, and the filters in the next section must allow the traffic. Routes and addresses decide direction, and N A T only works one way.

Routes decide where a packet can go. Filters decide whether it is allowed. A W S gives us two. A security group is attached to a network interface. It contains only allow rules, all of them considered together, and it is stateful: if a request is allowed in, its reply is allowed out automatically. A network A C L is attached to a subnet. It has both allow and deny rules, evaluated in order from the lowest rule number, first match wins, and it is stateless, so the reply needs its own rule, usually on the client's ephemeral ports. Most designs do their real filtering with security groups, and here is the shop's chain. The load balancer's group, s g a l b, allows port four four three from anywhere, because shoppers are anywhere. The app servers' group allows port eight zero eight zero, but only from s g a l b. Notice the source is not an address range; it is another security group, meaning any interface carrying that group. When the load balancer adds nodes, the rule still fits. The database group allows five four three two only from the app group. The request in the middle is exactly that app rule, validated against the E C two A P I. So the database cannot be reached even by something else inside the V P C that is not an app server. The misconception is that a route means traffic flows. A route is necessary, but every filter on the way, security groups and network A C Ls, in both directions where they are stateless, must also allow it. Routes say where; filters say whether.

Shoppers do not type addresses; they type shop dot example dot com. D N S turns that name into an address. The browser asks a recursive resolver, usually run by the shopper's network. If the resolver has no cached answer, it asks the root servers, then the dot com servers, and finally the authoritative servers for example dot com. Ours is a Route fifty three public hosted zone, the container for the domain's records. The answer comes back with a time to live, a T T L, and the resolver caches it for that long. The record on the right is how we publish the shop. It is an upsert, create or replace, of an A record for shop dot example dot com. But instead of a fixed address, it is an alias: it points at the load balancer's D N S name, and Route fifty three answers with the load balancer's current addresses, which can change. Evaluate target health means Route fifty three will consider whether the target is healthy. This request was validated against the Route fifty three A P I; the zone identifiers are placeholders. Below it are the routing policies, which decide which answer to give when there is more than one: simple, weighted, for sending ten percent of users to a new version, latency, failover to a secondary, and geolocation. The misconception is that a D N S change takes effect at once. Resolvers all over the world keep the old answer until its T T L expires. So treat names as cached pointers, and plan changes around their T T Ls.

So far we have made the request reachable. That says nothing about whether anyone on the path can read it. T L S does two jobs on a single hop: it encrypts the traffic, and, with a certificate, it proves that the server really is shop dot example dot com. A W S Certificate Manager, A C M, issues certificates for A W S endpoints and renews them automatically once the domain is validated, here through D N S. Look at the path. The browser's connection uses T L S one point three and ends at the load balancer. That is the termination point. The commands request the certificate and attach it to an H T T P S listener on port four four three with a T L S one point three security policy. The certificate must live in the load balancer's own Region, E U west two; CloudFront, by contrast, only uses certificates from U S east one. After the load balancer, the request travels to the app server on port eight zero eight zero, and unless the target group is set to H T T P S, that hop is plain H T T P inside the V P C. The database hop is encrypted only if the application's database client requires T L S. The table makes each hop a separate decision. The misconception is that traffic inside a V P C is encrypted anyway. Being able to reach something tells you nothing about encryption. So decide each hop explicitly, and write down where T L S terminates.

The load balancer is where many app servers become one service. An application load balancer understands H T T P, so it can route by path or host; a network load balancer forwards T C P and U D P with very low overhead. Behind a listener sits a target group, the set of servers that should receive traffic. Health checks decide which members actually get it. The command creates the shop's target group and sets every health check value explicitly rather than relying on defaults: check the slash health path every ten seconds, mark a target unhealthy after two failures in a row, and healthy again after three successes. Now the timeline, computed by the code with exactly those numbers. App three breaks at time zero. The checks at five and fifteen seconds fail, so at fifteen seconds it is marked unhealthy and traffic stops. Until then, roughly fifteen seconds of requests went to a broken server. It is fixed at sixty seconds, and three passing checks bring it back at eighty five seconds. Meanwhile the evening's five hundred and sixty requests a second are spread across fewer targets: about ninety three each across six, about one hundred and twelve each across five. Our servers handle one hundred and fifty, so the others absorb it. The misconception is that a failing target disappears instantly. The interval times the threshold sets the delay in both directions. So set those thresholds on purpose, and keep spare capacity for the moments a target is out.

The last piece of the network is private paths. Today, when the app servers read product files from S three, the traffic leaves through the N A T gateway, as if S three were any other internet service. A V P C endpoint gives it a private path instead. A gateway endpoint for S three adds a route to the subnet's table pointing at S three's address list, and it has no endpoint charge. Its endpoint policy, on the board, limits it to the shop's buckets, so the endpoint cannot be used to copy data somewhere else. It was checked against the I A M action and resource reference. Interface endpoints do the same for many other services, by placing a network interface in your subnet, with an hourly charge. Connecting networks to each other is next in the table. V P C peering joins exactly two V P Cs, like our route to the development V P C, and it is not transitive: if A peers with B and B with C, A still cannot reach C through B. A transit gateway is a hub for many V P Cs. To reach the shop's office network, a Site-to-Site V P N runs I P sec over the internet, with two tunnels per connection, and Direct Connect provides a private, dedicated link. The misconception is that Direct Connect is encrypted. It is private, but it is not encrypted by default; you add MACsec on supported links, or run a V P N over it. Every path has a boundary, whether transitivity, cost or encryption. With request paths established, next we choose where application processing runs and how capacity changes.

Our order A P I has to run somewhere, and A W S offers several homes for the same code. On E C two, we run the whole operating system: the most control, and the most work, because the patching is ours. On E C S with Fargate, we hand over a container image and A W S runs the hosts underneath it. On Lambda, we hand over a function; A W S runs everything else, and each invocation can last at most fifteen minutes. And on E K S, we run Kubernetes, which brings its own ecosystem and its own cost for every cluster hour. The table compares them on what you patch, the unit you scale, how you are billed, the longest a single run can last, and how long a new unit takes to start. None of these is best in general. The workload's shape decides. The order A P I serves steady H T T P traffic all day, up to five hundred and sixty requests a second at the evening peak, and it holds connections open to its PostgreSQL database. It is one service, owned by one team, deployed weekly. That points to containers on Fargate as a provisional choice: no operating system to patch, steady capacity, and connections that stay open. We will build both the virtual machine and the container version in this chapter so we can compare them honestly. The misconception is that serverless is always cheaper. Per request billing is excellent for spiky or idle workloads; for steady, heavy traffic it can cost more than capacity you keep busy. So let shape, control and effort decide, and write the choice down with its reasons.

If capacity must come and go, every server has to be reproducible. Two pieces make that possible. An A M I, an Amazon Machine Image, is the disk image an instance boots from. A launch template records everything else about how to start one. On the left is the order A P I's template, validated against the E C two A P I. It names the A M I and the instance type, m seven g large. It attaches the instance profile from chapter two, OrderApi, so the app gets temporary credentials with least privilege from the very first boot. It requires I M D S version two, the token based metadata service. It places the server in the app security group, carries a first boot script as user data, and tags every instance with its app and environment. When something changes, we create a new template version, here version fourteen for release one point four point two, rather than editing a running server. On the right is an instance's life. It starts pending, becomes running, and is billed per second while it runs. Stopping keeps its volumes, which are still billed, as we saw in chapter one. Terminating deletes it for good; a terminated instance cannot be started again. The misconception is that stopping is a cheap restart. A stopped instance keeps costing for its storage, and on start it may land on different hardware. So treat servers as copies of a template, and fix the template, never the copy.

An instance type name is a compact specification. Read m seven g large from the left. M is the general purpose family, balanced between C P U and memory; C would lean to compute, R to memory. Seven is the generation. G means a Graviton processor, which is Arm sixty four, so our code and our container images must be built for that architecture. Large is the size: two virtual C P Us and eight gibibytes of memory. Then comes a separate decision: how to pay for the capacity. The program prices one month of the order platform with the course's hypothetical rates, so treat them as placeholders. Three servers, one per zone, run all day, every day. That is a floor we are sure of, so it gets a one year commitment at thirty percent off: two thousand one hundred and sixty hours, sixty dollars forty eight. The evening peak adds three servers for six hours a day; that is less certain, so it stays on demand: twenty one dollars sixty. The product image worker can be interrupted and resumed, so it runs on Spot, spare capacity at a deep discount: three dollars eighty four. The mix comes to eighty five dollars ninety two, against one hundred and seventeen sixty if everything were on demand. The misconception is that Spot is free money. A W S can reclaim a Spot instance with a best effort two minute notice, so only work that tolerates interruption belongs there. Commit the floor, buy the peak on demand, and put interruptible work on Spot.

A template describes the server; something still has to turn a fresh instance into a working app server. That is the job of user data, a script that runs once, as root, on first boot. Read it top to bottom. It installs the Java runtime and the CloudWatch agent. It copies release one point four point two from the shop's release bucket, and notice there are no credentials in the script: the instance profile's role allows exactly that read. It configures the agent to ship the application's log files to CloudWatch Logs, so we have logs from the first minute. And it starts the service. Every line of this card was checked to parse as bash. Now operations. Traditionally, an operator would open port twenty two and keep an S S H key. Systems Manager removes both. With Session Manager, a w s s s m start session gives a shell through the agent on the instance; the security group needs no inbound rule, there is no key to leak, and access is decided by I A M and recorded. Patching works the same way: send command runs the A W S Run Patch Baseline document against every instance tagged as the order A P I. The list shows what remains ours on E C two: patching the operating system and the Java runtime, preferring to bake a new A M I over fixing servers by hand, keeping the log agent configured, and keeping the instance role narrow. The misconception is that A W S patches your instances. It patches the hosts underneath them; the guest operating system is yours. So bootstrap from a template, and operate through I A M, not keys.

An Auto Scaling group turns the launch template into a fleet. It keeps the number of instances between a minimum and a maximum, spreads them across the zones, and replaces any instance that fails its health checks. To change the size it needs a signal: target tracking, which keeps a metric near a target; step policies; or a schedule. Let's test reactive scaling against the shop's evening surge, with code. At eighteen hundred, demand climbs from two hundred and forty to five hundred and sixty requests a second over four minutes. The group starts with three servers, scales to keep twenty five percent headroom, sees its metric a minute late, and, by our assumption, a new server takes five minutes from launch to serving traffic. The result: five minutes in which demand exceeds capacity, at worst by one hundred and ten requests a second. Those are the slow pages and failed checkouts of the busiest moment of the day. Now the scheduled version. The surge is not a surprise; it happens every evening. A scheduled action raises the minimum to six at seventeen forty five, London time, and the request beside it was validated against the Auto Scaling A P I. With six servers already serving, the model is never short. Capacity is also not unlimited: a group cannot exceed its maximum, the account has quotas, and a zone can run short of a particular instance type. The misconception is that Auto Scaling is instant. Metrics arrive late and servers take minutes. So react to the unexpected, and schedule the expected.

Now the same order A P I as a container. The artefact is an image, stored in E C R, the Elastic Container Registry, and tagged with the release, one point four point two. E C S runs it as a task, from a task definition, which plays the role the launch template played for E C two. And an E C S service keeps a chosen number of tasks running, registers them with the load balancer's target group, and replaces any that fail. Read the task definition, validated against the E C S A P I. It requires Fargate, so A W S runs the hosts. It uses a v p c networking, so every task gets its own network interface in our app subnets and its own security group. It asks for five hundred and twelve C P U units, half a v C P U, with one thousand and twenty four mebibytes, a valid Fargate size, on A R M sixty four. Two roles appear, and they are easy to confuse. The execution role is used by E C S itself to pull the image and write logs. The task role is what the application's own A W S calls use, our least privilege OrderApi role. Logs go to CloudWatch through the a w s logs driver from day one. And stop timeout gives the app thirty seconds to finish work when E C S stops it. The table compares the virtual machine and container versions: the artefact, who patches the operating system, the unit of scale, start time, roles and logging. The misconception is that containers make an application stateless. They do not; only its design does, which is the last section of this chapter. Image, task definition and service together are the container's template.

Kubernetes is the most widely used container orchestrator, and E K S is A W S's managed Kubernetes. You declare what should run in manifests, like the deployment on the board, six replicas of the order A P I image on port eight zero eight zero, and Kubernetes keeps reality matching that declaration. E K S runs the control plane for you, but the cluster is still a platform you operate. There is a charge for every cluster hour, ten cents an hour on standard support and sixty cents once a version falls into extended support. Each Kubernetes version has about fourteen months of standard support, so upgrades are a recurring job. And nodes, networking add ons and the people who understand all of it are yours. The table sets out when that cost is worth paying: many services and many teams sharing one platform; an organisation already invested in Kubernetes tools; a need to run the same platform across clouds; or scheduling requirements that simpler services cannot express. Now the shop. It has one service, owned by one team, deploying weekly. E C S already gives it tasks, services, scaling, load balancer integration and per task roles. So the verdict is E C S for now, and to revisit the question when services and teams multiply. The misconception is that Kubernetes is the grown up default. It is a powerful platform, and a platform has to be operated. So adopt orchestration for requirements you have today, not for ones you might have one day.

Everything in this chapter assumes that servers come and go: scale in, failed health checks, Spot interruptions, deployments. That only works if no request depends on one particular server. The plan asks us to see what happens when that rule is broken, so the left program runs it. Three hundred shoppers are spread across three app servers, and each server keeps its shoppers' carts on its local disk. Then scale in terminates app two, a perfectly normal event. Ninety nine of three hundred carts are gone. The same carts kept in a shared store that every server can reach, like the cache or database of chapter six, lose nothing. The second program is the other half: shutting down well. When E C S or Auto Scaling stops a task or instance, the process first receives a SIGTERM signal. The worker handles it: it finishes the job in hand, order forty one, stops taking new work, and leaves orders forty two and forty three on the queue for another worker. Then it exits cleanly. If it ignores the signal, E C S waits for the stop timeout, thirty seconds by default and at most one hundred and twenty, then sends SIGKILL, and whatever was half done is lost. Spot gives a best effort two minute warning first. The misconception is that a replaced server means a recovered business. Auto Scaling restores capacity, but it does not bring back the ninety nine carts. Process recovery is not business correctness. So keep state outside the server, and treat shutdown as a normal event. Replaceable compute needs deliberate storage choices, so next we separate transient execution state from persistent data.

Chapter four made servers disposable, which raises the obvious question: where does the data live? A W S offers three interfaces to bytes. Object storage, S three, stores whole objects under keys and is reached over an H T T P S A P I; you replace an object rather than editing bytes inside it. Block storage, E B S, is a disk attached to one server, living in one Availability Zone, where you can change any byte. File storage, E F S, is a shared directory that many servers mount over N F S at the same time. Read the table for the shop. Product images and order exports are written once and read by many, from anywhere, so they go in S three. A server's local scratch space or build cache belongs on an E B S volume. Invoice P D Fs that several workers create and read together belong on E F S. The list on the right asks the persistence question that chapter four left open. Instance store disappears when the instance stops. An E B S volume survives its instance but not the loss of its zone. S three and E F S survive the loss of a zone. The misconception is that storage is storage and only the price differs. The interface, the scope and the way updates work are different, and an application written for one does not simply work on another. So for every kind of data ask three things: who reads it, how it changes, and what it must outlive.

Shoppers can attach a photo to a product review, and those bytes should not travel through our app servers. S three can take them directly, without making anything public. First the vocabulary. A bucket holds objects, and an object's key is its full name, such as reviews slash p one thousand and one slash photo seventy seven dot j p g; the slashes are part of the name, not real folders. Every request to S three is authorised, by I A M policies, bucket policies, and the account's block public access settings. The trick is a presigned U R L. Follow the sequence on the left. The browser asks the order A P I for permission to upload. The A P I, whose role is allowed to put objects under reviews, signs a single request: a put to that exact key, for three hundred seconds. The browser then sends the photo straight to S three, which checks the signature, the expiry and the policies. The code on the right really signs such a U R L with placeholder credentials. It prints only the parameter names, because the date and signature change on every run: the algorithm, the credential scope, the expiry of three hundred seconds, a security token, because the signer used temporary credentials, and the signature. That token matters. A presigned U R L stops working at its expiry or when the signing credentials expire, whichever comes first. The misconception is that uploads need a public bucket. They do not; keep every bucket private and grant single, short-lived requests instead.

S three is strongly consistent: once a write has succeeded, every later read and every listing sees it. That is a promise about reading. It is not a promise about two writers. Here is the case the plan asks for, run in an emulator. A pricing job and a stock job both read product p one thousand and one's file, at the same version. The pricing job lowers the price to ten; the stock job reduces stock to thirty nine. Both write the whole object back. With plain puts, S three applies them in order and the last writer wins. Look at the first output line: the price is back at twelve. The price change was silently lost, and no error was raised anywhere. Now the same race with conditional writes. Each job sends If Match with the E Tag it read. The pricing job's write matches and succeeds. The stock job's write no longer matches, because the object changed, so S three refuses it with Precondition Failed. The stock job re-reads, re-applies its change and writes again. The final object has both changes: price ten, stock thirty nine. If None Match, with a star, is the companion: create this key only if it does not exist yet. One boundary remains. All of this is per object. If an update must change p one thousand and one's file and the catalogue index together, S three has no transaction across the two keys; a reader can see one without the other. The misconception is that strong consistency makes shared writing safe. It makes reads safe. Use conditional writes for races, and never assume atomicity across keys.

Versioning changes what overwrite and delete mean. With versioning on, an overwrite keeps the previous version, and a delete without a version I D does not remove anything; it adds a delete marker on top. Follow the emulated timeline. We write the product at twelve, then at ten, then delete it. A plain get now returns no such key, so to applications the object is gone. But listing the versions shows one delete marker and both versions still kept. Removing the delete marker itself, by its version I D, undoes the delete, and the latest version, price ten, is back. That history is not free. Every old version is stored and billed, which is where lifecycle rules come in. The rule on the right, validated against the S three A P I, expires noncurrent versions after thirty days. A second rule ages the order exports: to Standard Infrequent Access after thirty days, and to Glacier Flexible Retrieval after ninety. Storage classes trade price for conditions. Infrequent Access charges per retrieval and has a thirty day minimum. Glacier Instant Retrieval and Flexible Retrieval have ninety day minimums, and Deep Archive one hundred and eighty. Flexible Retrieval and Deep Archive also need a restore before you can read, taking minutes to hours, or up to two days for Deep Archive. The misconception is that Glacier is simply cheaper S three. It is cheaper storage with minimum durations and slower, paid retrieval. Versioning is your history; lifecycle decides how long you keep it and where it lives.

Block volumes have a boundary we met in chapter one: an E B S volume lives in one Availability Zone and can only attach to instances in that zone. If the zone is lost, so is the volume's availability. Snapshots are the way across. A snapshot is a point in time copy of a volume, stored Regionally, and later snapshots store only the blocks that changed, so they are incremental. To recover, you never repair the old volume; you create a new volume from a snapshot, in any zone you choose. The program runs that sequence in an emulator. It creates a thirty gibibyte g p three volume for the invoice service in E U west two a. It takes the nightly snapshot, which completes and belongs to the Region rather than a zone. Then, imagining zone a is lost, it creates a new thirty gibibyte volume from that snapshot in E U west two b, ready to attach to a replacement server there. Two cautions come with real E B S that an emulator does not show. First, a volume restored from a snapshot loads its blocks lazily from storage the first time they are read, so early reads are slow, unless you pay for fast snapshot restore in that zone. Second, a snapshot only contains what was on disk at that moment; data written after it, or still in an application's memory, is not there. The misconception is that a restore is instant and complete. Plan for the warm up, and for the data since the last snapshot. Volumes are zonal; snapshots carry data between zones.

Some applications genuinely need a shared directory. The shop's invoice workers generate P D F invoices that other workers read and bundle, and they run in all three zones. E F S fits. It is an N F S file system for Linux, Regional rather than zonal, with a mount target in each zone, so every worker mounts the same slash m n t slash invoices from its own zone. It grows and shrinks with the files stored. The request on the board, validated against the E F S A P I, creates the file system with the general purpose performance mode, elastic throughput, which scales with demand, and encryption at rest, which is chosen at creation time. When the protocol or the workload is different, F S x offers managed file systems built for it. The table maps needs to choices. Windows file shares over S M B, joined to Active Directory, go to F S x for Windows File Server. Scratch space for very high throughput computing goes to F S x for Lustre. Teams that rely on NetApp features use F S x for O N T A P, and those that want Z F S snapshots and clones use F S x for Open Z F S. The misconception is that you can just share an E B S volume. A volume belongs to one zone and, except in special multi attach cases, to one server at a time. So choose E F S for shared Linux files, and F S x when the protocol or the performance profile demands something else.

The last storage question is protection, and it is where similar sounding features are most often confused. Start with encryption. The request on the board, validated against the S three A P I, makes the shop reports bucket encrypt every new object with a K M S key, alias shop reports, and enables a bucket key to reduce key requests. With K M S, reading an object needs permission on the key as well as on the object, which adds a second, separate gate. Now the table, which crosses threats with protections. Replication copies new writes to another bucket, perhaps in another Region, so it protects against a zone or Region outage. But by default it does not replicate delete markers, and an accidental overwrite or a corrupt write replicates faithfully. Versioning protects against accidental deletes and bad overwrites, because history remains, but anyone allowed to delete versions can delete history too. Object Lock in compliance mode blocks deletion until the retention period ends, even for the root user, so it stops an attacker who has stolen credentials. A backup is a separate copy, ideally in another account or Region, that you can restore from. Notice the last row: none of these stops someone who can read the data from reading it. That is access control's job. The misconception is that replicated means backed up. A replica is a mirror, mistakes included. And the evidence for recoverability is a restore you have actually performed. Storage preserves bytes; next we examine database services that organise application state and coordinate changes.

Databases differ less in what they can store than in which questions they answer well. So before choosing one, write down the questions. An access pattern is a question the application asks, how often it asks it, and how fast it needs the answer. Read the shop's list, at the evening peak. Product pages read one product by its I D, around four hundred and fifty times a second, and a slightly old answer is acceptable, so they are cacheable. Placing an order happens only around six times a second, but it must be all or nothing: the order, its items and the stock reduction must happen together or not at all. A customer's order history is read by customer, newest first. Stock must never go below zero. And sales by day is a nightly scan over history, which belongs to the analytics chapter. Three data models answer these differently. Relational databases hold tables you join and query flexibly with S Q L, with strong transactions. Key value databases fetch items by key at very high scale, with queries you design in advance. In memory caches hold short lived copies for speed. Finally, growth: how many rows and bytes in three years, not today, because the choice must survive success. The misconception is to pick the database first and fit the queries to it afterwards. It works the other way: the queries pick the database. So write the patterns down, then compare the models against them.

The orders data is relational: orders, items, products and stock, joined and changed together in transactions. We could install PostgreSQL on an E C two instance ourselves, but R D S runs it for us. R D S is a managed relational service for several engines: PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, Oracle and SQL Server. Aurora is A W S's own design for MySQL and PostgreSQL compatible engines, built on a distributed storage layer that keeps six copies of the data across three zones. Read the request, validated against the R D S A P I. It creates shop orders on PostgreSQL sixteen, on a d b m seven g large instance with one hundred gibibytes of g p three storage. Multi A Z is on, so a standby waits in another zone. Storage is encrypted. Automated backups are kept for seven days, and deletion protection stops an accidental delete. Notice the password. Manage master user password asks R D S to create the password and keep it in Secrets Manager, so it never appears in code, configuration, or this request. The database sits in the data subnets behind the database security group from chapter three. The table shows who does what. R D S and Aurora take on installing and patching the engine in your maintenance window, backups and point in time recovery, and failover. Your schema, your S Q L, your indexes, and who may connect remain yours. The misconception is that managed means tuned. A missing index is just as slow on R D S. So R D S manages the engine, and you still own the data model.

Now the order itself, run for real in PostgreSQL sixteen. The script creates products, orders and order items, with one rule on products: stock must never go below zero. Order five hundred and one asks for two of product p one thousand and one, and two of p one thousand and two, of which only one is left. All of it runs inside one transaction. The first stock update succeeds. The second would make stock negative, so the check constraint raises an error, and the database aborts the whole transaction. The output proves it: stock is still forty and one, and there are zero orders. No half order exists anywhere. That is what a transaction buys: the database, not our code, guarantees all or nothing. The right side is a different kind of failure. Every app server keeps a pool of connections, here twenty each, and every connection counts against the database's maximum, two hundred in our assumed parameter group, minus ten reserved for administration. Three, six or nine servers fit. Scale to twelve for a sale and two hundred and forty connections are wanted, so fifty are refused with too many clients, exactly when traffic is highest. R D S Proxy addresses this by pooling and sharing connections in front of the database, and the credentials come from Secrets Manager, not from code. The misconception is that retrying fixes a failure. If the order committed but the reply was lost, a blind retry creates a second order. Retries need an idempotency key, which chapter seven builds. Let the database enforce the rules, and budget connections like any other capacity.

Four database capabilities are routinely blurred together, and the plan asks us to keep them apart. A Multi A Z D B instance deployment has one standby in another zone, kept in step synchronously, and not readable; if the primary fails, R D S fails over to it, typically in about one to two minutes. A Multi A Z D B cluster has two standbys that can serve reads, and A W S says failover is typically under thirty five seconds. Aurora shares one storage volume, six copies across three zones, among a writer and up to fifteen replicas. A read replica is a different thing again: it is asynchronous, it serves reads, it can lag behind the primary, and promoting it is a deliberate step, not an automatic failover. And backups with point in time recovery let you restore to any second within the retention window, from one to thirty five days, but always as a new instance. Now two incidents at five past six in the evening. First, a zone is lost. Multi A Z fails over, and no data needs restoring. Second, a deployment runs an update that sets every price to zero. The standby received that update synchronously; it is just as wrong. The only answer is a point in time restore to four minutes past six, into a new instance, and then switching the application to it. The misconception is that Multi A Z is a backup. It copies every mistake instantly. Availability, read scaling and recovery are three separate decisions, each with its own evidence.

DynamoDB is a key value and document database that serves single digit millisecond reads at almost any scale, provided the keys match the queries. Every item has a partition key, which decides where the item is stored, and optionally a sort key, which orders items that share a partition key. Our pattern was a customer's orders, newest first. So the partition key is the customer, and the sort key is the order time followed by the order number. The program, run in an emulator, writes twenty orders across eight customers and then asks for customer c seventy seven's two newest orders in a single query, reading backwards along the sort key. No scan, no join. A global secondary index, a G S I, re-keys the same items for a different question: here, orders by status. It finds the two pending orders. But look at the last line. Status has only two values, so eighteen of twenty items share one partition key value in that index, PAID. At real scale, every write lands on that same key, and a single partition key value has a throughput limit. That is a hot partition. Capacity can be on demand, paying per request, or provisioned, but either way it needs to be spread across many distinct key values. The misconception is that you can index any attribute and query it freely. An index on a low cardinality attribute concentrates load. So choose partition keys with many distinct values, and use sort keys to order within them. This was a single Region table with on demand capacity; other variants change the guarantees, as the next section shows.

The relational database enforced stock with a check constraint inside a transaction. DynamoDB has its own tools for the same rule. A condition expression attaches a test to a write, and the write is refused if the test fails. A transaction groups several writes so they all succeed or none do. The program, run in an emulator, sells the last unit of product p one thousand and two twice. Each attempt is one transaction with two parts: put the order item, and decrement stock on the condition that stock is at least one. Order six oh one succeeds: the order is written and stock goes from one to zero. Order six oh two fails with conditional check failed, and because it was a transaction, its order item was not written either. The final line reads stock with a strongly consistent read: zero, and one order. Consistency in DynamoDB depends on where you read, which is why the plan asks us to name the variant. On a table, a default read is eventually consistent and may briefly miss a recent write; asking for a consistent read returns the latest. A global secondary index offers only eventually consistent reads. Global tables, replicated across Regions, come in two variants: with multi Region eventual consistency, concurrent writes in different Regions resolve as last writer wins and strong reads are only current for writes made in your Region; with multi Region strong consistency, writes are confirmed in another Region before they succeed. The misconception is that DynamoDB reads are always current. Indexes and default reads are not. Use conditions to guard rules, and name the variant before promising consistency.

Four hundred and fifty product reads a second do not all need to reach the database. A cache such as ElastiCache, holding copies in memory, can answer most of them. The common pattern is cache aside. The application reads the cache first. On a hit, it uses the copy. On a miss, it reads the database and fills the cache, with a time to live, a T T L, after which the copy expires. The program plays the price of product p one thousand and one through two timelines, with a sixty second T T L. In the first, nothing happens to the cache on a write. At zero seconds a read misses and caches twelve. At ten seconds the price in the database drops to ten. At twenty and at fifty nine seconds, readers still get twelve from the cache: stale. Only at sixty one seconds, after expiry, does a read fetch ten. For almost fifty seconds, shoppers saw the wrong price. In the second timeline, the write also deletes the cache key, so the next read misses and fetches the new price. That closes the window, but not perfectly: a reader that fetched the old value just before the write can put it back into the cache just after. Short T T Ls bound that case. The misconception is that a cache is just a faster database. It is a second copy of the data, and copies can be wrong. So decide how much staleness each kind of data can tolerate, invalidate on write where it matters, and always bound the rest with a T T L.

The shop did not start in A W S. Its original orders database runs on premises, and it must move to R D S without stopping sales for a weekend. The Database Migration Service, D M S, is built for that. A migration task first performs a full load, copying every existing row, and then keeps applying change data capture, every new insert, update and delete, until the target has caught up. Then you cut over, switching the application's writes to the new database, with a plan to switch back if something is wrong. The command on the board creates such a task, orders to R D S, with the migration type full load and C D C, and its parameters were checked against the D M S A P I. The table mappings select every table in the shop schema. When the source and target engines are the same, as PostgreSQL to PostgreSQL, the schema moves as it is; between different engines, the schema has to be converted first. Before cutover, validate: row counts, a sample of totals, and the latest order numbers on both sides. The lower table marks the boundaries of specialist databases: graph queries many hops deep point to Neptune, full text and log search to OpenSearch, years of analytics to Redshift, durable microsecond reads to MemoryDB, and the MongoDB A P I to DocumentDB. The misconception is that every need deserves its own database. Each one is another system to secure, back up and operate. Migrate with change data capture, and specialise only for a real access pattern. Durable application state now supports workflows that cross service boundaries; next we connect requests, events, and background work.

Until now, shoppers reached the order A P I through a load balancer. For an A P I built from functions, A P I Gateway is the front door, and it can enforce three things before any of our code runs. First, the contract. The J S O N schema on the left says what a valid order looks like: an I D starting with o dash, and at least one item, each with a product and a quantity of at least one. The commands register it as a model and attach a request validator, so a malformed body is rejected at the door. Second, identity. A Cognito authoriser checks the shopper's token on every request. Third, rate. Stage throttling caps the A P I at six hundred requests a second, and A W S also applies account level defaults, ten thousand requests a second steady with a burst of five thousand, per Region. The card at the bottom shows what callers see. An order with an empty items list gets four hundred, invalid request body. A request without a token gets four oh one. The six hundred and first request in a second gets four twenty nine, too many requests, which tells a well behaved client to back off and retry. One more limit matters: a R E S T A P I integration times out after twenty nine seconds by default, so long work does not belong behind a synchronous call. The misconception is that validation is the handler's job. The handler should still be careful, but rejecting bad input at the edge costs nothing and protects everything behind it. Contract, identity and rate, enforced at the edge.

A Lambda function is code that A W S runs when an event arrives, inside an execution environment it creates and manages. Two parts of the code run at different times. Everything at module level, outside the handler, is the INIT phase. It runs once, when a new environment starts. Here it loads the product prices and sets a counter. The handler runs once per event, and an environment handles one event at a time. After an event, Lambda may keep the environment warm and reuse it for the next one, skipping INIT. The program runs the handler locally with a test event, exactly as the A P I would send it. It returns status two oh one with the order and a total of twenty nine, the same total as chapter six. Watch the counter. In a warm environment the first call sees one and the second sees two, because module state survived. Then we simulate a new environment, and the count is back to one. Real traffic spreads across many environments, created and discarded as A W S sees fit, so that counter is meaningless as a business number. The request on the right creates the function: Python three point one three on arm sixty four, five hundred and twelve megabytes, its own execution role, and a timeout of ten seconds set explicitly. If a call exceeds it, the invocation is stopped. Our examples assume a standard on demand function. The misconception is that a global variable remembers things. It remembers only until that environment goes away. So cache expensive setup in INIT, and keep state that matters in a database.

Lambda scales by running more environments at once, and the number running at any moment is its concurrency. There is a simple law for it: concurrency equals the request rate times how long each request takes. The program applies it to place order, assuming each invocation takes about point one two seconds. At sixty requests a second, about seven environments are busy. At two hundred and forty, about twenty nine. At the five hundred and sixty request peak, sixty seven. Now remember chapter six. Each environment holds a database connection, and the database has only one hundred and ninety to spare. So we cap the function. Reserved concurrency fifty, the request beside the program, means place order can never run more than fifty at once, and it also guarantees those fifty out of the account's pool, which starts at one thousand per Region. At the peak, that cap throttles about one hundred and forty three requests a second with four twenty nine, which clients retry with backoff, and the database never sees more than fifty connections. Whether that trade is right is a business decision; the point is that it is now a decision rather than an outage. The execution role beside it is least privilege, checked against the I A M reference: put and get on the idempotency table, and put events on the default event bus. Nothing else. The misconception is that serverless scales without limits. The function might; the things it calls do not. So cap concurrency to what your dependencies can take.

A queue lets one part of the system hand work to another without waiting for it. The fulfilment service will read order events from an S Q S queue. Consumers poll the queue and receive messages. A received message is not removed; it becomes invisible for the visibility timeout, thirty seconds by default, up to twelve hours. If the consumer finishes, it deletes the message, and the delete is the acknowledgement. If it does not, the message becomes visible again and someone else receives it. The program plays this in an emulator, with a one second timeout so it runs quickly. Worker A receives order five oh one, receive number one, and crashes before deleting it. Worker B polls immediately and sees nothing, because the message is invisible. After the timeout, worker B receives the same message, receive number two, processes it and deletes it, and nothing is waiting. Notice what that means: the work was attempted twice. Set the visibility timeout longer than processing takes, or one slow worker will cause a second. Standard queues deliver at least once, with best effort ordering and very high throughput. F I F O queues keep order within a message group, such as one customer, and deduplicate repeated sends within a five minute window. The misconception is that F I F O means exactly once. It suppresses duplicate sends for five minutes; a consumer that crashes before deleting still causes a second delivery. So delete only after success, and design every consumer to expect redelivery.

A queue gives each message to one consumer. Often several services care about the same event: fulfilment must ship the order, loyalty must award points, and fraud checking wants to look at large orders. That is fan out, and S N S does it. You publish once to a topic. Every subscription receives its own copy. A subscription can carry a filter policy, so it receives only the messages it cares about. The common pattern, shown on the board, is a topic in front of queues: each consuming service gets its own S Q S queue, so a slow or broken consumer builds up its own backlog without slowing the others. The program builds exactly that in an emulator. The order events topic has three queue subscriptions. Fulfilment and loyalty take everything. Fraud check has a filter policy on the message attribute total: numeric, greater than or equal to five hundred. Three orders are published, totals twenty nine, six hundred and forty, and seventy five. Fulfilment and loyalty each receive all three. Fraud check receives only order five oh two. Filtering happens in S N S, so the fraud service never pays to receive and discard the others. The misconception is that several services can simply read the same queue. They would compete: each message would go to one of them. So fan out with a topic, and buffer each consumer with its own queue.

S N S filters on message attributes chosen by the publisher. EventBridge goes further: it routes on the content of the event itself, from many sources, through rules. Producers put events onto a bus. Each event has a source, a detail type, and a detail object with the facts. A rule is a pattern; when an event matches, EventBridge invokes the rule's targets, such as a queue, a function or a workflow. The program defines two rules in an emulator. U K VAT matches order placed events from the shop's orders source whose country is G B. Refunds matches order refunded events from any country. Three events are put on the bus. Order five oh one, placed in G B, reaches the U K VAT queue. Order five oh two's refund reaches the refunds queue. Order five oh four, placed in France, matches no rule, and nothing receives it. That is correct behaviour, but it is easy to miss: an event no rule matches is simply not delivered anywhere. The structure of detail is now a contract. The VAT service depends on a field called country, spelled that way. If the orders team renames it, routing silently stops. EventBridge can record schemas so producers and consumers agree on that shape. The misconception is that events are fire and forget. The producer forgets; the consumers depend on every field. So route on content with rules, and version the schema like any other A P I.

Some business processes are several steps that must happen in order: reserve the stock, charge the payment, ship the order. Chaining functions that call each other hides that process in code. Step Functions makes it explicit as a state machine, which keeps the workflow's state between steps and records every execution. The diagram and the definition on the right are the same workflow, and the definition's structure was checked: every next and catch target exists, and every task has a resource. Reserve stock calls a function and retries if Lambda is throttled, waiting one second, then two, then four, because the backoff rate doubles the interval, up to three attempts. Then charge payment. If the payment provider declines, that is not a transient error worth retrying. The catch sends the workflow to release stock, which undoes the reservation, and then to a fail state that records why. That undo step is compensation: there is no transaction across the stock service and the payment provider, so we design the reverse action ourselves. Step Functions has two workflow types. Standard workflows can run for up to a year and execute each step once. Express workflows run for up to five minutes, at much higher rates, and can run steps more than once, so their steps must be idempotent. The misconception is that retries make a process reliable. Retries handle transient failures; a permanent failure halfway through needs an undo. So retry the transient, and compensate the permanent.

Everything in this chapter delivers at least once. Queues redeliver, Lambda retries, clients time out and try again. So the effect of handling something must be safe to repeat. That property is idempotency: doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once. The program shows the two duplicates the plan asks about, in an emulator. In both, the protection is a record keyed by an idempotency key, written with a condition that the key does not exist yet. First, a fulfilment message delivered twice. The first delivery claims ship o five oh one and ships a parcel. The second finds the key already there and does nothing, so one parcel is sent. Second, a timeout after a successful write. The shopper's app posts an order with idempotency key k ninety one. The order commits as five oh one, but the reply is lost. The app retries with the same key, and instead of creating order five oh two, the A P I returns five oh one again. Neither case would be caught by F I F O deduplication, which only suppresses repeated sends within five minutes. Retries also need backoff with jitter, so a crowd of clients does not retry in lockstep, and a limit, after which the message goes to a dead letter queue for inspection and later replay.
