Who retries depends on how Lambda was invoked, as the table shows: for synchronous calls, the caller; for asynchronous events, Lambda itself, twice more; for a queue, the message reappears until its receive count sends it to the dead letter queue. The misconception is that deduplication equals idempotency. Deduplication is the transport's feature; the business effect is yours. Record the key with the effect, and replay becomes safe.

The last section assembles the chapter. Each mechanism answers a different need, and a real system combines them. Follow an order through the board. The shopper posts the order and waits, because they need to know whether it was accepted, so that hop is synchronous: A P I Gateway to the place order function. That function does the minimum that must be true before answering: it checks the idempotency key, writes the order in one database transaction, and replies. Only after the commit does it put an order placed event on the event bus. Publishing before the commit would announce orders that might still roll back. From the bus, the work fans out. The payment and stock process is a Step Functions workflow, because its steps need an order and a way back. Fulfilment reads from its own queue, so a warehouse outage builds a backlog rather than losing orders. Other consumers, such as loyalty and VAT, attach their own rules or subscriptions without the orders team changing anything. The table is the summary: a synchronous A P I when the caller needs the answer now, a queue for one consumer and smooth bursts, a topic to fan out the same message, an event bus to route by content from many sources, and a workflow for ordered steps with compensation. The misconception is that making everything asynchronous is always more scalable. The shopper still needs an answer, and an asynchronous accept you cannot keep is worse than a clear error. Use synchronous calls for answers, asynchronous messages for work, and workflows for processes. Operational events also support analytical views; next we follow data into systems designed for broader queries.

Everything so far served the live shop: small, fast reads and writes of the current state. Analytics asks different questions. How many orders were paid but not yet shipped at eight in the evening? What were sales by day last month? Those questions scan a lot of data, they care about history, and an answer a few minutes or hours old is usually fine. The program shows why the operational database cannot answer them. The orders table keeps only the current state: o five oh one is shipped, o five oh two is paid, o five oh three is placed. But the question was about twenty hundred. Replaying the history of changes up to that moment gives a different answer: o five oh one and o five oh two were both paid and not yet shipped, because five oh one only shipped at half past nine. The current state has overwritten that fact. So analytics keeps its own copy, built from every change. The board shows the pipeline this chapter builds: order changes flow out of the orders database into an S three data lake, a Glue catalog describes the files as tables, and Athena runs S Q L over them. The misconception is to just query production. A long scan for a report competes with checkout for the same database, at exactly the times both are busiest. Keep history separately, and query it without touching the orders database.

Getting operational data into the lake can be done in several ways, and the table lists them. A nightly batch export is simplest when yesterday is fresh enough. Change data capture, for example with the D M S task from chapter six, sends every insert and update within minutes. A stream carries events in seconds. And bulk transfer moves files from on premises. Whichever you choose, two things will happen. Records will be duplicated, because pipelines retry and replay. And records will arrive late. The program processes the twelfth of October as it actually arrived. Six records came in. Order five oh two's first change appears twice, a replay. Order five oh four's change happened at two minutes to midnight but only arrived at four minutes past, in the next batch. Deduplicating by order and sequence leaves four unique orders. Placing each by its event time, not its arrival time, keeps five oh four on the twelfth. Then the step most pipelines skip: reconciliation. The source database says four orders totalling seven hundred and fifty six pounds fifty for that day; the lake agrees, so the day is published. Had they disagreed, the day would be held back and investigated. The misconception is that a successful job means complete data. A job can succeed while missing a late file or counting a replay twice. So deduplicate, place records by event time, and reconcile against the source before anyone reads the numbers.

Once data is in S three, its layout decides how much every query has to read. Three ideas matter. Columnar formats such as Parquet store each column together, so a query that needs only the date and the total reads only those columns. Partitioning puts files into folders by a value you often filter on, like dt equals the twenty sixth of September, so a query for one day can skip every other folder. And file size matters, because every file carries its own metadata and costs a request to open. The program measures all three on a seeded month of order history, sixty thousand rows, written as Parquet three ways. A query for the twelfth of September opens six hundred and twenty nine kibibytes when the data is unpartitioned, because it must look at everything. With date partitions, it opens twenty four kibibytes, about twenty six times less. Then the same single day written as two hundred tiny files, which is what a stream writing every few seconds tends to produce: two hundred and twenty kibibytes and two hundred file opens, for the same two thousand rows. The fix for small files is compaction, a job that rewrites them into fewer, larger ones. The misconception is that storage is cheap, so layout does not matter. Storing it is cheap; reading it is what you pay for, on every query. So use Parquet, partition by how you filter, and keep files sensibly sized.

Files in S three are just objects. To query them as tables, something must describe them, and that is the Glue Data Catalog. The request on the board, validated against the Glue A P I, creates the order history table in the shop lake database. It records the location in S three, the columns, order I D and total as a decimal with two places, the partition key d t, and that the files are Parquet. That is all it is: metadata, a claim about what the files contain. Glue jobs, typically Spark, do the transformation work: converting raw C D C files into partitioned Parquet, and compacting small files. Schema changes are where the claim and reality drift apart. If the upstream team renames total to amount, the files change but the catalog does not, and queries start returning nulls rather than errors. A crawler or the job itself must update the schema, deliberately. Now the table of three promises, which the plan asks us to keep apart. Where the data is and what shape it has is the catalog's job. Who may read which tables and columns is enforced by I A M and Lake Formation, which can grant at column and even row level. Whether the rows are right, complete and not duplicated is a data quality job, like the reconciliation in section two. The misconception is that a table in the catalog is therefore governed and correct. It is only described. The catalog describes, permissions enforce, and checks verify.

With the files laid out and catalogued, Athena can query them. Athena is serverless S Q L over S three: there is no cluster to run; you send a query, it reads the files the catalog points to, and it writes the result to S three. Athena is not available in this course's environment, so the program runs the same standard S Q L in DuckDB, a local engine, over the same date partitioned Parquet files, and the card says so. Read the query as an analyst would. It counts orders and sums sales per day, for the eleventh to the thirteenth of September, grouped and ordered by date. The result has one row per day: two thousand orders each, with sales of two hundred and two thousand two hundred and twenty four pounds fifty two, two hundred and five thousand six hundred and seventeen thirty nine, and two hundred and two thousand eight hundred and seventy six fifty. Because the where clause filters on the partition column, only three of thirty date folders are read. The command below submits the same query to Athena, in the analysts workgroup, which can cap and report usage. Athena bills by bytes scanned, published at five dollars per terabyte with a ten megabyte minimum per query; treat the rate as an example and check current pricing. The misconception is that adding a limit makes a query cheap. A limit cuts the rows returned, not the bytes scanned to find them. So filter on partitions, and select only the columns you need.

Some data cannot wait for a nightly batch. The shop's clickstream, every product view and add to basket, feeds near real time recommendations. A stream carries it. Which Kinesis service matters, so let's be precise. Kinesis Data Streams stores records in shards. Each record has a partition key, and ordering is guaranteed only within a shard, so only per key. Each shard accepts up to one megabyte or one thousand records a second, and records are kept for twenty four hours by default, extendable to a year. Consumers read at their own pace, and the distance between the newest record and where a consumer is reading is its iterator age. Kinesis Data Firehose is a different service: it buffers incoming records and delivers them to destinations such as S three, with no consumer code to write. The program models the evening on a provisioned stream with two shards. At eighteen hundred, fifteen hundred clicks a second arrive, and the consumer, handling sixteen hundred, keeps up. From half past six, eighteen hundred a second arrive. The shards can accept that, but the consumer cannot process it, so a backlog builds: by half past seven, over a million records, about eleven minutes behind. When traffic drops at twenty hundred, it drains. Nothing is lost, because the backlog never approached the twenty four hour retention. But recommendations were eleven minutes stale at the busiest moment. The misconception is that data in the stream is data processed. Watch the iterator age. Size shards for what comes in, and consumers for what must go out.

The last choice is the processing engine, and it should come from who consumes the data, not from which engine is most impressive. Three engines can sit over the same lake. Athena runs ad hoc S Q L, billed per scan, with nothing to keep running. Redshift is a data warehouse: it keeps data in managed storage optimised for repeated analytical queries, and it serves many concurrent dashboards with consistent performance. E M R runs managed Spark and Hadoop clusters for processing that needs custom code at large scale; the Spark course covers that engine in depth. Read the selection table for the shop. A few analysts asking new questions each week: start with Athena. Fifty dashboards refreshed every hour for the whole company: a warehouse such as Redshift, because the same queries repeat all day. Building machine learning features from years of clickstream: E M R with Spark. A monthly C S V for finance: an Athena query and an export. These are provisional choices, revisited when the consumers change. The list underneath says what to check before adding any engine. Keep one copy of truth, the catalogued lake, rather than several diverging copies. Remember that every engine is another bill, another set of roles to secure, and another thing to monitor. And let the freshness each consumer actually needs decide between batch and streaming. The misconception is that a bigger engine is a better one. Each one adds cost and operational work. Keep one lake of truth, and choose engines per consumer. The application and data paths are understandable; next we make their infrastructure and releases reproducible.

Every resource in this course so far could be created by hand or with a script of commands. That works once. The second time, in another account or after someone changed something, it starts to fail. Compare the two cards. On the left, a script: create the dead letter queue, look up its A R N, create the main queue pointing at it. It is a list of actions to perform, in order. Run it twice and the second create either fails or produces something subtly different, and nothing records which resources belong to this system. On the right, the same two queues as a CloudFormation template. It does not say what to do; it says what should exist: a dead letter queue, and a queue whose redrive policy points at it. CloudFormation works out the steps, and a stack, the deployed instance of the template, owns everything it declares. The table shows what that buys. Running it again changes nothing if nothing changed. Ownership is recorded. Deleting the stack deletes its resources together. And the same template builds the same system in the development account and in production. The list adds the principles: describe the end state, let the engine derive the order from references, give every resource exactly one owning stack, and review templates like code, in pull requests. The misconception is that any script is infrastructure as code. A script records actions; a template records the intended state. Declare the end state, and let one stack own it.

Let's read a real template, the order events plumbing from chapter seven, linted with cfn lint. Each entry under resources has a logical name, such as order events queue, a type, such as A W S S Q S Queue, and properties. The interesting part is how resources refer to each other. Ref returns a resource's main identifier; for a queue, its U R L, for a topic, its A R N. Get att returns a named attribute, such as the dead letter queue's A R N. Every reference is also a dependency: CloudFormation cannot create the main queue until the dead letter queue exists, because it needs that A R N for the redrive policy. The queue policy allows only the S N S service to send messages, and only when the source is our topic, the same scoping we discussed for services in chapter two. The program on the right takes those references and computes the creation order with a topological sort, which is what CloudFormation does internally. Wave one creates the topic and the dead letter queue at the same time, because neither depends on anything. Wave two creates the queue. Wave three creates the queue policy and the subscription, which need both. Deletion runs the same waves in reverse. When a dependency exists that no reference expresses, depends on makes it explicit. The misconception is that resources are created from the top of the file to the bottom. Order in the file means nothing; the references are the dependency graph.

The same template must build development and production, which differ in a few values. Those are parameters. The template on the left takes an environment, restricted to dev or prod, and an image tag, and uses them to name a configuration parameter and a secret, so slash shop slash prod and slash shop slash dev never collide. Outputs publish values for other stacks, and an export makes one importable by name. Notice what is exported: the secret's A R N, never its value. Secrets are where templates most often go wrong, so the program asks a tool rather than trusting a rule of thumb. It runs cfn lint on two versions of the orders database template. The version with the master password typed into the template is flagged with rule W twenty five oh one: passwords should not be hard coded. The version that asks R D S to manage the master password in Secrets Manager has no findings. In the template on the left, the payments A P I key is likewise generated inside Secrets Manager; its value never appears in the template, in parameters, or in any build log. When a template must use an existing secret, a dynamic reference resolves it at deployment time instead. The misconception is that marking a parameter no echo hides it. No echo masks it in some displays, but values in outputs and metadata are not masked, and anything printed in a pipeline log is visible to whoever can read the log. Use parameters for configuration, and references for secrets.

Before updating a stack, CloudFormation can create a change set: a preview listing each resource that would be added, modified or removed, and whether a modification happens in place or by replacement. Replacement is the line to look for. It means CloudFormation creates a new resource with a new identity, points the stack at it, and deletes the old one. For a queue, that is a new U R L every consumer must learn. For a database, it is a new, empty database unless you move the data yourself. Which properties force replacement is not folklore; it is in A W S's resource provider schemas, as create only properties. The program reads those official schemas, bundled with cfn lint, and predicts the outcome of the shop's version fifteen template. Changing the database's instance class or its backup retention updates the instance in place, although some in place changes still interrupt service briefly. Turning on storage encryption replaces the database. Renaming the queue replaces the queue. The table sets out the limits. A change set tells you which resources change, and how. It does not tell you whether the update will succeed: a quota, a name already in use, a missing permission or a service error can still fail it. It says nothing about your data. And it cannot see changes someone made by hand in the console; that is drift, and drift detection compares live resources with the template. The misconception is that a change set that previews cleanly guarantees a clean deployment. It is a preview. Read it for replacements, and detect drift before you deploy.

Updates fail. When one does, CloudFormation rolls the stack back to the last version that worked. Read the illustrative events. At eighteen forty, version fifteen starts updating. The queue updates. The order A P I service never becomes stable, because its new tasks fail their health checks, so its update fails. CloudFormation rolls the stack back and, a few minutes later, version fourteen is restored. That sounds like a complete undo, and it is not. At eighteen forty and twenty seconds, the new release's schema migration added a column to the orders database. Rollback restores resources and their configuration; it does not reverse what the application did to data, emails it sent, or payments it took. So the database needs protection from the stack itself. The template, linted with cfn lint, sets the deletion policy and the update replace policy to snapshot, explicitly: if the stack is deleted, or the database is replaced, CloudFormation snapshots it first. The update replace policy defaults to delete, which is exactly the trap from the previous section, where enabling encryption would replace the database. Deletion protection adds a second lock: R D S refuses delete requests, whoever sends them. The misconception is that rollback undoes everything. It undoes the stack. So set protection policies explicitly on every stateful resource, and make schema changes backward compatible, so the old version still works if the new one is rolled back.

Infrastructure is one half of delivery; releasing new application versions is the other. A pipeline builds an artefact once, here a container image, and deploys it using its own role, never a person's credentials, so every change is attributable and repeatable. How the new version meets traffic is a strategy. With blue green, the new version, green, runs beside the old one, blue, and the load balancer shifts traffic between them. Canary shifts a small slice first and the rest later; linear shifts in equal steps. Combined with an alarm on errors, each limits how much traffic a bad release can reach. The program puts numbers on it. Version one point five point zero, unknown to us, fails two percent of requests. An error alarm fires two minutes into the deployment and triggers a rollback. At five hundred and sixty requests a second, shifting everything at once fails one thousand three hundred and forty four requests before the rollback. Linear, ten percent every minute, fails two hundred and two. A ten percent canary fails one hundred and thirty four. And because blue was never stopped, rollback is just moving traffic back. The command starts such a deployment with CodeDeploy, using the predefined configuration that shifts ten percent every minute. The misconception is that good testing makes an all at once deployment safe. Production traffic finds what tests miss. Shift gradually, watch the alarms, and keep the old version ready.

The last step is getting a change from development to production without letting anything slip in between. The rule is to promote the artefact, not the build. Commit nine f three c two e one is built once into an image with a fixed digest, a hash of its exact contents. That same digest is deployed to dev, tested, and then deployed to prod. Rebuilding for production would pull dependencies again and could produce a different image from the same code. Provenance is the record that links them: which commit, which build, which digest, deployed where and when. Identities are separated too. The pipeline runs in the development account with its own role. In production, a deploy role trusts only that pipeline role, and the trust policy on the board, checked against the I A M reference, says exactly that. The Developers group from chapter two has read only access in production, so no person deploys there directly; every change to production arrives through the pipeline. Finally, the tools. CloudFormation, which we used, takes Y A M L or J S O N. The A W S C D K lets you write the same stacks in a programming language and synthesises CloudFormation from them. Terraform uses its own language and keeps its state in a file you must store and protect. Each is a reasonable choice; mixing them for the same resources is not. The misconception is that rebuilding for production is harmless because the code is the same. Builds are not perfectly repeatable. Build once, record it, and promote it with narrow roles. Reproducibility supports operations but does not establish health; next we connect telemetry, incident response, and recovery evidence.
